one_liner: Per-class bump arena behind class-specific operator new/delete; book run shows about 1.3x faster construction than new/delete.
what_it_does: SizeBasedArena<T, N> is a singleton that mallocs room for N objects of type T once and hands out consecutive sizeof(T) slots. A class opts in by overloading its own operator new/delete (and new[]/delete[]) to call the arena, so call sites keep writing new Orc and delete p unchanged. The chapter10 programs build up to it in steps: a hand-written Tribe arena reached through a Meyers singleton, the same with a global static singleton, the templated SizeBasedArena, and a safer variant that requires T to be final.
how_it_is_fast: Allocation is a pointer bump (cur += sizeof(T)) under a std::mutex, with no size-class lookup, no per-object header and no call into malloc after the first one. Deallocation is an empty function, so freeing is free; the global-singleton variant lets the compiler delete the whole free loop, which is where the book's 0 us delete figure comes from. Objects are packed contiguously at sizeof(T) stride (16 bytes for Orc), so the timed loop touches fewer fresh pages than glibc's header-carrying chunks.
when_to_use: Single-class, allocate-many-then-drop-all phases (a level's entities, a parse tree, a batch job) with a known lifetime cap on the number of objects created.
Retrofitting an existing class whose call sites use plain new/delete, by adding four class-level operator overloads.
Teaching or prototyping region allocation before moving to a production arena such as std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource.
when_not_to_use: Any workload that creates more than N objects over the program's life, even if few are alive at once: delete never returns space and allocate_one has no bounds check, so object N+1 writes past the malloc'd buffer.

Class hierarchies: operator new ignores its size argument and hands out sizeof(T) slots, so a larger derived class overruns the next slot unless you use the -safer variant (static_assert(std::is_final_v<T>)).
Multithreaded hot allocation paths: every allocation takes the arena's single std::mutex.
Memory-sensitive code: N * sizeof(T) bytes (16 MB for 1,000,000 Orcs) are reserved up front and released only when the singleton dies at program exit.
Anything that needs a general allocator; it serves one type and is a book example, not a maintained library.

integration.dependencies: none (standard library <mutex>, <cstdlib>, <cassert>; <type_traits> for the safer variant)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 for the arena (class template argument deduction in std::lock_guard, std::is_final_v in the safer variant); the test drivers use C++23 <print>. Book build was online gcc 15 at -O2 per the record.
integration.thread_safety: allocate_one/allocate_n are serialised by one std::mutex; the Meyers-singleton construction is thread-safe function-local static initialisation; deallocate is a no-op.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — call sites keep new/delete unchanged for the one class that overloads its operators, but delete never frees and capacity is fixed at N objects for the whole run

gotchas: No exhaustion check: past N lifetime allocations the arena silently hands out memory beyond its buffer (heap overflow), unlike a pool that falls back to ::operator new.

Array new differs by variant: the Tribe versions' operator new[] is assert(false) with no return statement (undefined behaviour under NDEBUG); SizeBasedArena's version computes n / sizeof(T) and so assumes the compiler adds no array cookie, which holds only for trivially destructible T such as Orc.

Singleton choice changes timing: with the Meyers singleton the 16 MB malloc happens inside the first timed new and every call pays a static-guard check (the 638 us delete loop); the global static member avoids both but is exposed to static initialisation order if another translation unit's static initialiser news the class.
The book's delete comparison is glibc free() against an empty function the optimiser can drop, so the 8.03% and 0 us delete ratios measure doing nothing, not a faster free.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when you want the smallest possible per-class arena with unchanged call sites; ArenaAllocator (privateMwb) has a real benchmark against std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource, and obstack (cleeus) or fast-alloc are better choices when you need arena or pool code with published measurements.
verified_claims_summary: In the book's single run (online gcc 15, -O2 per the record, CPU not stated), constructing 1,000,000 16-byte Orc objects took 23,433 us through libstdc++ operator new (glibc malloc) versus 17,906 us (Meyers-singleton arena) and 17,573 us (global-singleton arena), about 1.3x; destroying them took 7,943 us with free() versus 638 us and 0 us for the arena's no-op delete. The repo carries the five driver programs (identical loops, only the operator overloads differ) but no results, build line or CPU, and the arena side still pays a mutex per allocation and first-touch page faults inside the timed loop.
status_note: MIT-licensed Packt companion repository (87 stars) with commits through 2026-08-14, but the chapter10 arena files are unchanged since their 2024-08-14 upload; tiny and copyable, best treated as a worked example rather than a library.
